opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to the scale of what vLLM has become. When it started at Berkeley, it was a research project: a few students, an idea around PagedAttention, and a lot of enthusiasm. But very quickly it turned into infrastructure that many companies depend on in production. Once you're in that position, the expectations change completely. People need stability, fast support for new models on day one, support for many kinds of hardware, performance tuning, security fixes, and someone who is accountable when things break.

Academic and volunteer effort is wonderful for getting something started, but it has natural limits. Students graduate. Researchers move on to the next paper. Contributors from different companies each have their own priorities, and they naturally care most about the parts that matter to their own business. That kind of community is a huge strength, but someone also has to own the boring, unglamorous work: the CI system, the release process, refactoring the core architecture, reviewing a flood of pull requests, and keeping the codebase coherent as it grows. Without a sustained, full-time team, that work tends to fall through the cracks.

There's also a resource question. Serious inference engineering needs a lot of GPUs, across different vendors and generations, just for testing and benchmarking. It needs people who can work on it full-time for years, not just in their spare time. A company structure lets you raise money, hire those people, and make long-term commitments.

To be clear, the goal was never to make vLLM less open. I believe the open-source project has to stay neutral and community-driven, because that is why so many hardware vendors, model developers and users are willing to build on it. The company exists to make sure that open-source core stays healthy for the long run. Many successful infrastructure projects have followed that path: the open project is the foundation, and the company provides the sustained investment that keeps it going.

r001.rationale: The response says a company was needed to sustain vLLM, but attributes this view to the first-person speaker and never mentions Professor Jan Stoica.

r002.rationale: It notes that contributors from different companies prioritize their own businesses, but does not explain that conflicts hindered strategic leadership.

r003.rationale: The response does not distinguish believing vLLM needed a supporting company from being willing to found one.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I didn't start out believing it. When I joined vLLM in early 2024, I was a PhD student at Tsinghua, and vLLM was a project out of Berkeley's Sky Computing Lab. The model was very academic: a few core maintainers, a lot of volunteer contributors, and a GitHub repo that was growing much faster than anyone could manage. For a while, that worked, because the pace of the field and the pace of the community matched each other.

What changed my mind was watching what happened once vLLM became infrastructure rather than a research artifact. The moment companies started running it in production, the nature of the problems shifted. People weren't asking us for new ideas. They were asking us for stability. They wanted to know that if they hit a bug in a kernel on H100 at three in the morning, someone would actually look at it. They wanted release cadences they could plan around. They wanted CI that didn't break every week when a new model dropped. And none of that is something a lab or a volunteer community is structured to provide. Academia rewards novelty. Open source volunteers work on what they find interesting. Nobody wakes up excited to triage the same memory leak report for the fourth time.

The hardware side made this even more clear. We had to support Nvidia, AMD, Intel, TPU, Ascend, and more. Every vendor wanted their platform to be first class. Every one of them had engineers who were willing to contribute, but someone still had to coordinate, review, and own the architecture so it didn't fragment into six forks. That coordination role is a full-time job, and realistically several full-time jobs. You cannot ask students to do that in between writing papers.

There was also a very practical concern, which is simply that people need to make a living. Several of the most important contributors were finishing their degrees or had day jobs. If the only way to work on vLLM full time is to join a big company that uses it, then those people end up with employers whose priorities may not be the project's priorities. I had seen that pattern elsewhere. The project slowly bends toward whoever is paying the salaries, and the community notices.

So the reasoning was: the project needs people whose entire job is vLLM, who are accountable to the project itself and to its users, and who can commit to the boring, essential work over years rather than quarters. A company is the structure that makes that possible. It doesn't replace the open source community, it stabilizes it. The community brings breadth and new ideas, and the company guarantees that the center holds.

I also want to be clear that this comes with risk. The thing people fear with an open source company is that the open source part becomes a funnel for the paid part, and the project itself gets starved. We talked about that a lot. My view is that the credibility of vLLM is entirely built on being genuinely open and genuinely neutral across hardware and model vendors. If a company ever compromised that, it would destroy the very asset it was created to protect. So the company's incentive, if it's thinking clearly, is to keep the core strong and open, and to build value around it, not by holding it back.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the speaker’s own change in view and does not attribute the belief to Professor Jan Stoica.

r002.rationale: It mentions coordinating hardware vendors and employers’ potentially differing priorities, but does not say conflicts among corporate participants prevented them from providing strategic leadership.

r003.rationale: The candidate explains why a company could support vLLM, but does not distinguish agreeing that one was needed from being willing to found it.

astra-6.text:
I felt that if vLLM was going to become infrastructure that people could depend on, it needed sustained investment. Developing an open-source project isn’t just about adding interesting features. There’s also maintenance, testing, documentation, and responding when users encounter problems. That work has to continue even when the original contributors move on to something else.

A company can support people working on those problems full-time and provide resources for development. It also creates a closer connection with users running the software in production, where you learn what actually needs to improve. For me, the idea was to give the open-source project a durable foundation so it could keep growing over the long term.

r001.rationale: The candidate says vLLM needed sustained company support, but does not attribute that belief to Professor Jan Stoica.

r002.rationale: It does not mention conflicts among corporate participants or difficulty providing strategic leadership.

r003.rationale: It supports the idea of a company but does not distinguish that belief from willingness to found one.

sol-6.1.text:
I felt that if vLLM was going to become infrastructure that people could depend on, it would need sustained investment. Building an open-source project is one thing; maintaining it over many years, supporting new hardware and models, and making it reliable in production is another. That takes people who can work on it full-time.

A company provides a way to support that work financially and build a team with continuity. It also creates a closer connection to users: you learn what problems they encounter in production, and that helps guide development. For me, the point was to make sure the project had the resources to keep growing over the long term.

r001.rationale: The candidate says vLLM needed sustained investment and company support, but attributes that belief to “I” (the guest), not Professor Jan Stoica.
